results.title: 5 Best Practices for Writing Reproducible Code in R
results.content: # 5 Best Practices for Writing Reproducible Code in R. Reproducible code is an integral part of modern data science. In R, there are several best practices you can follow to make your code more reproducible and more straightforward to collaborate on. In this article, we’ll look at 5 best practices to help you write reproducible R code. my_project/ │ ├── data/ # Raw and cleaned data ├── R/ # R scripts or functions ├── output/ # Plots, tables, results ├── reports/ # R Markdown reports or presentations ├── README.md # Project overview └── .Rproj # RStudio project file. For example, use the **here** package to refer to project files like so:. Clear documentation is key to making your code understandable and reproducible. You can use the **roxygen2** package to document functions directly within the code:. This file should explain the project’s purpose, the data used, and how to run the code. It helps other users understand your work quickly and set up the environment for running the code. Version control is essential for keeping track of changes in your code and collaborating with others. Version control also makes it easy to revert to previous versions of your code if something goes wrong. If you’re working with others, GitHub or GitLab helps you to share your code and track issues. Setting up a consistent environment ensures your code runs the same way on any computer. In R, you can use the renv package to manage your project’s environment. It tracks the versions of the packages you use and helps others set up the same environment. Anyone else working on the project can restore the same environment by running:. When your code involves random processes, such as random sampling or model initialization, the results can change each time you run it. Writing reproducible code is not only a good practice, but it also ensures that your work can be easily shared, verified, and built upon. By following these five best practices—using project-oriented workflows, documenting your code, using version control, setting up a consistent environment, and setting a seed for randomness — you make your code more reliable and easier for others to replicate.

results.title: Best Practices for Creating Reproducible Experiments in MLOps
results.content: Published Time: 2023-05-24T09:31:36.561Z Best Practices for Creating Reproducible Experiments in MLOps Reproducibility in Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) is critical for ensuring reliability and consistency in data-driven experiments. In this article, we will explore some of the best practices that data scientists and machine learning practitioners can implement to create reproducible experiments in MLOps. 1. git init # Initialize a new Git repository # Add all relevant files to the repository git commit -m "Initial commit" # Commit the changes Creating isolated and reproducible environments for experiments is another best practice. To ensure reproducibility, it is essential to set random seeds for all components involving randomness, such as random initialization, data shuffling, or model selection. Implementing a system for tracking and logging experiment details, including hyperparameters, model configurations, evaluation metrics, and training/validation data splits, is another best practice. Using tools like continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines to automate model training, evaluation, and deployment processes reduces variability and ensures that experiments can be easily reproduced consistently. Containers ensure that models can be consistently reproduced across different systems, maintaining the same behavior as during the training phase. RUN pip install -r requirements.txt Implementing checkpointing mechanisms to save intermediate model states during training allows resuming training from a specific point, ensuring reproducibility even if the training process is interrupted. Facilitating collaboration and reproducibility by sharing code, data, and trained models with proper documentation is vital. Making use of code repositories, data versioning systems, and model registries provides a centralized and accessible repository for others to reproduce and build upon your work. In conclusion, reproducibility is a vital aspect of MLOps that ensures experiments can be consistently replicated and validated. Implementing best practices such as version control, environment management, reproducible data pipelines, experiment tracking, documentation, workflow automation, containerizing models, checkpointing and versioning mechanisms and sharing and collaboration can enhance collaboration, facilitate troubleshooting, and promote the credibility of your work.

results.title: Best Practice for good documented reproducible analysis - General - Posit Community
results.content: CLICK HERE to read the announcement blog post. until now, my analysis were kind of messy big .R files. Today i´m interested in your workflow and how you make your analysis good documented and reproducible. My idea is: i would probably create a new rstudio project file, use an .rmd file for the whole report, but would do the analysis in seperate .r files which then are called within the .rmd file - chunk via source(). * one .R file for loading libraries (perhaps with needs()-package?). * one .R file for loading data and data-cleaning. * one .R file for Plot1. * one .R file for Table 2 and Plot2. How do you make sure, your code still runs when r-packages get updated? 3. put it under privat version control via github (only the scripts/ not the data). 4. use subfolder structure R for scripts and data with subfolders input/output for data. 5. my first r script is usually called 00\_main. 7. the first script is usually 01\_install\_and\_load\_libraries. Install calls are afterwards outcommented, so that I just make library calls when I source this scripts. The 2nd script usually contains helper functions, which I need during the whole analysis. 8. in the following scripts I load and clean the rawdata. In these scripts I usually implement tests, change datatypes and introduce naming conventions. The sourcing of the preprocessing is afterwards outcommented in the main file. (In other kind of projects at this step would also be stuff like importing data from a database). 9. the next scripts I load the preprocessed/clean data. usually logical stuff happens in the loading script. When possible I try to load the data in a way, that I have a general setting for all upcoming analysis steps. The next part is the analysis. And normally don't run 2 analysis without restarting r in between. For the next analysis I start with 07\_ etc. The output of these analysis is written in subfolders organized like data/output/results/06\_analysis/... In the first script of each analysis I document what questions I want to answer, how the analysis is organised, critical steps, etc.

results.title: Artifact Evaluation for Reproducible Quantitative Research | SIGARCH
results.content: In this blog post, we discuss “*Artifact Evaluation*” to foster wider adoption of computer architecture ideas. The software community can point to many examples of wider adoption facilitated by sharing research artifacts (code, data, scripts, etc.). To stimulate artifact dissemination in the software community, over the past 6 years we have helped introduce and standardize the so-called Artifact Evaluation (AE) process at many top software ACM, IEEE and NeurIPS conferences such as PPoPP, CGO, PACT, Supercomputing and SysML. The committee performs lightweight validation of submitted artifacts based on the standard ACM procedure we contributed to a few years ago: check if the artifact is permanently archived, follow its installation instructions and verify functional correctness, partially replicate results from the paper, assign reproducibility badges, etc. Finally, the community has even started discussing how to share reusable artifacts and crowdsource experiments via public repositories to help new research easily build upon past research, thus truly enabling open science. At the same time, AE allows the authors to receive important feedback and fix problems in a friendly and cooperative way before making their artifacts more widely available. 3. Architecture artifacts are way more complex than software ones, and therefore are simply too hard or time-consuming to package for AE. For example, AE does not mandate the authors to make their artifacts publicly available: we have found multiple ways to evaluate artifacts without revealing all the IP. We will have much more to say about fair benchmarking in our future posts, but we believe that introducing AE for architecture research would go a long way in addressing this issue. First, by making their artifacts available through AE the authors will reduce the effort for other researchers to reproduce their results and hence invite more objective comparisons. In conclusion, we should remind ourselves that while AE does place a greater burden on the authors, it leads to wider adoption of their research ideas (with all the good things that come with it). Making artifacts available in a common reusable format allows other researchers to easily build upon them, which implies that the burden of AE can be gradually reduced over time even for complex, quantitatively-oriented artifacts typical for architecture research.

results.title: bridging-the-gap-between-offline-and-online-reinforcement-learning-evaluation-methodologies - Ask this paper | Bohrium
results.content: **研究方向：**Offline RL ｜ Sequential evaluation ｜ Sample efficiency. Offline RL methods use pre - collected data to start the learning process. There is also a lack of consensus on evaluation protocols in the offline RL community. This paper proposes to evaluate algorithms based on available data rather than just final performance or learning curves over gradient steps. Current offline RL algorithms often constrain the agent's policy around dataset - seen behavior. In RL, considering its non - stationary data and the importance of sample efficiency, evaluating offline RL by data efficiency is proposed. Sequential Evaluation of Offline RL Algorithms. The traditional way of evaluating offline RL by multiple training epochs over the dataset has issues such as not showing sample efficiency well, hiding policy distribution changes, and making it hard to compare with online RL. It addresses the issues of epoch - style training and has benefits like providing information on algorithm scaling, visualizing behavior with dataset quality shifts, and enabling seamless evaluation of online fine - tuning. Several existing offline RL algorithms were evaluated using the sequential approach on the D4RL benchmark which has different environments and versions of offline datasets. A sequential style of evaluation for offline RL methods was proposed, where algorithms are evaluated as a function of data. Existing offline methods were compared using this evaluation. Sequential evaluation shows promise for the offline RL community. Offline RL algorithms try to address this issue by bootstrapping the learning process from existing logged data without needing to interact with the environment from the very beginning. While online RL algorithms are typically evaluated as a function of the number of environment interactions, there exists no single established protocol for evaluating offline RL methods.In this paper, we propose a sequential approach to evaluate offline RL algorithms as a function of the training set size and thus by their data efficiency. Sequential evaluation provides valuable insights into the data efficiency of the learning process and the robustness of algorithms to distribution changes in the dataset while also harmonizing the visualization of the offline and online learning phases. We compare several existing offline RL algorithms using this approach and present insights from a variety of tasks and offline datasets.
